title: Agents for Everything Else — swyx
talk_summary: swyx describes how a 9-person team runs a $9M+ conference business by giving non-technical staff direct access to a coding agent (Devin) for website building, CMS/schedule management, ETL, and ad-hoc research/purchasing. The core claim is that agents remove yak-shaving and blocking dependencies, so humans (including non-engineers) self-serve work and do more of it.

takeaways.what_they_do: Give non-technical teammates (designers, ops) direct access to the coding agent so they can execute ideas without waiting on engineers or contractors.
takeaways.numbers: 9 full-time people, >$9M revenue; 207 replies on one agent thread

takeaways.what_they_do: Replace a CMS/SaaS with a code repo as the single source of truth, then let the agent edit that code for routine data changes (schedule, speaker updates).
takeaways.evidence_quote: the unlock happened when I threw away the CMS and just kind of committed that to code, but use that code as my sort of source of truth

takeaways.what_they_do: Handle incoming requests by forwarding the raw artifact (email, screenshot) to the agent with a one-line instruction, no reformatting.

takeaways.technique: Agents for yak-shaving and dependency crawling
takeaways.what_they_do: Route dependency-install and setup yak-shaves to agents rather than humans, treating parallelism (not just autonomy) as the productivity source.
When replacing a tool/SaaS with agents, enumerate the top three stakeholder concerns and reduce them one by one rather than dismissing them.
